## A derivative from first principles

Let $f(x)=x^2$. Starting with the definition,

$$
f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h}
=\lim_{h\to 0}(2x+h)=2x.
$$

The derivative describes the local rate of change. At $x=3$, the slope is $f'(3)=6$.

## An integral

The corresponding antiderivative gives

$$
\int_a^b x^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{b^3-a^3}{3}.
$$

For example, $\int_0^1 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x=1/3$.

## A useful identity

For vectors $u,v\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality states that

$$
\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i v_i\right|
\leq\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i^2}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_i^2}.
$$

Equality holds when the vectors are linearly dependent.
